title: What temperature does to a chatbot's next word
summary: Temperature divides the model's scores before they become odds. Low sharpens the odds, high flattens them, zero always takes the top word.

beats.say: Same prompt, same model, and the answer can change every run.
A model scores every possible next word, then picks one.
A setting called temperature divides those scores before they become odds.
Take made up odds: seventy, twenty and ten percent.
Lower the temperature, and the top word pulls ahead.
Raise it, and the odds flatten out.
At zero, the model always takes the highest odds word.
Even then, small variations can still occur.
Temperature adds no knowledge. It only reshapes the odds.
Low is focused. High is varied.

facts.claim: Google's documentation says temperature controls the degree of randomness in token selection, and a temperature of 0 means the highest-probability tokens are always selected
facts.note: Vertex AI docs, Content generation parameters: 'Temperature controls the degree of randomness in token selection'; 'A temperature of 0 means that the highest probability tokens are always selected'

facts.claim: Google's documentation says low temperatures give more predictable output and high temperatures more varied output, and that small variations can still occur
facts.note: Same page: low values suit focused answers, high values give more varied or creative output; responses are mostly deterministic but small variations can still occur

facts.claim: Hinton et al. define the softmax with temperature as q_i = exp(z_i/T) / sum_j exp(z_j/T), and say a higher T produces a softer probability distribution
facts.note: arXiv 1503.02531, Equation 1: q_i = exp(z_i/T)/sum_j exp(z_j/T); 'Using a higher value for T produces a softer probability distribution over classes'

facts.claim: The example odds are made up; temperature 0.5 and 2 are applied by raising each odd to the power 1/T and renormalizing, which equals dividing the scores by T
facts.note: Derived from Equation 1: p_i is proportional to exp(z_i), so exp(z_i/T) is proportional to p_i^(1/T); 70/20/10 -> 90.7/7.4/1.9 at T=0.5 and 52.3/28.0/19.8 at T=2
